changes.text: The island now copes with several things at once. The newest one takes the big spot, and the rest become small bubbles beside it that keep their state: dictation, apps opening, and the same kind stacked into one bubble. A song change, a finished download or an update has its moment and then leaves on its own.

Notifications in the island stack up as cards behind the newest one. Each new one drops in from the top like a card dealt onto the pile, and the others step back. Resting the pointer on the stack spreads it into a list that stays on screen however long it gets; scroll it with the wheel or by dragging a card up or down. Flick a card sideways to dismiss it, click its close mark or right click it, or use clear all to send them all off at once.

The music card in the island takes its colours from the cover art, and a title too long to fit scrolls instead of wrapping. Clicking it turns the island itself into the media controller: its whole body grows into the card while the cover, the title, artist and album, the equalizer, the progress wave and the buttons each travel to their place, and a new island forms at the top. Resting the pointer on the music gets the controller ready, so the click starts the move straight away.
The dictation line in the island is one smooth curve that fades out at both ends.

The island's overview shows the weather under the date, from wttr.in every 30 minutes. weather.show set to false in config.json turns it off; weather.location, weather.units and weather.minutes set where, which units and how often.
A pinned island no longer takes the keyboard, and the screen around it stays clickable while it is open.
With the media controller open, the island still opens when the pointer rests on it, and clicks on it reach the island instead of closing the controller.

The hotkey sheet draws a whole keyboard: the function row, Print Screen and its neighbours, the Insert and Home block, the arrows as an inverted T and the numpad when anything on it is bound. ISO and ANSI are both drawn properly, and the ISO Enter is one stepped key instead of two boxes.
Dropdowns in Settings open again. Clicking one used to show an empty list.

Settings › Hotkey sheet › Board offers ISO, ANSI and Custom. Custom unlocks VIA layout and VIA keymap: Import lists the VIA files in your Downloads folder and nothing else, and Browse opens the system file picker. Every file you pick gets a short check, then a note under the row says this is it or this is not it, and why.
Try a sample board works again after you forget the sample, and an imported board has an open button so you can edit its file into your own board. The sheet follows your edits as you save.
Split is no longer offered under Board. If you had it chosen, the sheet keeps drawing it and the list shows it until you pick something else.
The list on the left of Settings folds down to its icons with the button at its bottom, and the settings beside it get the room. It stays folded until you unfold it.

When the shell restarts, it puts back what you had open: the launcher or any other panel, a pinned sidebar menu, quick controls, notifications, the island, the on-screen keyboard and the Files window in its folder. Settings reopens on the same page, with the same rows expanded, scrolled to the same place, and the calculator keeps its number. A reboot or logging out still starts you with nothing open.

The lock screen is new. It covers the whole screen with your wallpaper blurred behind it, a large clock, the date and a password field, and nothing of the shell shows through. It grows out of your desktop when it locks and folds back into the password field when you unlock.
A wrong password is turned down at once instead of after about two seconds. A password you send while the last one is still being checked waits its turn instead of being dropped.
The lock screen shows how many notifications are waiting, with the apps they came from but nothing they say, and what music is playing. Point at the music to pause it or skip a track.
The password field shows your keyboard layout when you have more than one, and clicking it switches. It says so when Caps Lock is on, and an unplugged laptop shows its battery under the field.
Move the pointer to the bottom of the lock screen for sleep, restart and shut down. Each needs a press held until its ring fills, so a stray click does nothing.
After 10 seconds without a key or the mouse, the lock screen dims and its clock turns thin. Any key or movement brings it back.

lock.dim in config.json now sets how dark a veil sits over the lock screen's wallpaper, where it used to darken the picture itself, so the same number leaves your wallpaper more visible than before. New lock keys: font (the lock screen's typeface, Adwaita Sans by default), clockShare (clock size), clockLayout (row or stacked), restAfter (seconds before it dims) and verdict (milliseconds before an unanswered password counts as wrong).

banditshell dev try now lists each worktree with its pull request, open, merged or closed, and first clears away every worktree whose work is already on main, along with its branch. A worktree with changes of its own is never cleared. banditshell dev tidy does the same clearing without trying anything.
When a worktree you are trying gets merged, the shell goes back to main by itself within two minutes and sends a notification. A worktree that still has unsaved changes stays on.

In the banditshell dev try list, main is number 0 and the one running is marked * instead of a number. Picking the one already running says so instead of restarting it; banditshell restart still reloads it. In a terminal, the list and the messages are in colour.
notch.trackWidth in config.json no longer does anything, because the notch it sized is gone. The island that replaces it keeps its settings under island, and the new kernel check reads packages.

The notch at the top of the screen is now the island, a floating pill at the top centre. Opening an app, dictation, a finished download, a shell update and a new kernel all show up in it. Dictation no longer follows the focused window. Resting the pointer at the top centre still opens it, now with the clock, what is playing and anything still waiting for you.
Notifications can drop from the island instead of the top-right corner. Pick island under Sound › Notifications › Show them. The corner stays the default and opens the history either way.

The island tells you when a new Linux kernel is waiting. Pressing it runs sudo pacman -Syu in a terminal, or the command you set in System › Updates, and once the new kernel is installed it asks you to restart. The check needs pacman-contrib.
Finished downloads show up in the island if inotify-tools is installed. You can turn them off under Sound › Notifications › The island, along with the cover it shows when the track changes.
banditshell panel notch is now banditshell panel island. The old name still works.

The launcher's second style has a new name, alphabet. A config.json that still uses the old name for launcher.concept, or for the launcher's size settings, is moved over by itself the first time the shell starts. A script or keybind that sets the old name needs alphabet instead.

Settings you changed back when the panel said "nothing behind it in the shell yet" are carried into config.json once and now take effect. For example, a do not disturb switch you left on now really silences popups. Choices that belong to the system or to Hyprland, such as keyboard layouts or the power mode, start from what your machine has now. Settings you never touched keep behaving as they did: the lid, idle locking, alert sounds and startup apps change nothing until you choose something.

Every setting in Settings now does what it says. In Connections, the hotspot and VPN tunnels switch on and off through NetworkManager, and Add a tunnel imports a WireGuard .conf or OpenVPN .ovpn file.

Do not disturb works: popups and sounds stop while notifications still collect, it can end in an hour, at 18:00 or tomorrow morning, and it can come on every night. Alarms can still get through, and so do low battery warnings. Each app can have its own popup, sound and lock screen rule. Modes (work, play, stream, sleep) now change their settings and put them back when you leave, and banditshell focus switches modes and quiet from a terminal or keybind.
Alert sounds play for notifications, low battery and errors when you turn them on, in a soft, clear or wood set at their own volume. They start off.

Night light can follow a schedule, at set times or from sunset to sunrise for your time zone, easing in over a few minutes. Less motion, larger text and more contrast now apply to the whole shell. The 24-hour clock and the date style reach every clock and date the shell shows.

Display › Screens can turn a screen off or mirror another one. Like the other screen changes these wait for Apply and come with the countdown to go back. The last screen that is on cannot be turned off.

The sidebar can show the clock stacked, small, on one line or not at all, the date as day and month, day or nothing, and each status icon, the tray and the special workspaces can be hidden. A hidden status icon's menu still opens from its keybind. The active mode shows its icon above the status icons.
Volume past 100% is a switch. The launcher can forget what it learned, the clipboard imports clipse's history the moment you press Import, and the wallpaper reveal replays from its button.

Window layout, keyboard layouts, key repeat, mouse and touchpad speed, natural scrolling and tap to click are written to your Hyprland config, behind the existing permission to edit Hyprland files. Pen buttons can be remapped. The hotkey sheet draws an ansi, iso or split board, and an imported VIA keymap lights the keys the shell binds.

Power mode, what closing the lid does, the low battery warning level and what happens when the battery is nearly empty are real settings. Holding the battery's charge needs a small helper installed once with bash install.sh --charge-limit. Lock, screens off and sleep after a time of no use are off until you pick a time, and stand aside when hypridle or swayidle already does it.

Default apps and startup apps are real. Startup apps lists what starts from Hyprland, systemd, ~/.config/autostart and your own autostart launcher, and switches each off where it lives. Time zone, language and formats change the system's, asking for your password. Restore from a file shows what would change before anything is written, OBS's address and password can be set here, and the terminal's colours can follow the theme.
In Display › Screens, the arrangement snaps back to start at the top-left corner when you let go of a screen, instead of drifting further off with every drag.

When your Hyprland config fails Hyprland's own check, the shell now says so and changes nothing, instead of writing an edit and quietly undoing it. Edits made close together wait their turn instead of being dropped, and a screen edit lands in the right place on every machine that shares the config.

Updating no longer stops at a file you edited yourself. If an update changes a file you also changed, your edit is set aside in git stash first and the update goes through, and the update menu names the files. git stash list shows them and git stash pop brings them back. Edits to files the update does not touch stay where they are.
An open special workspace shows its apps' icons again. Before, the card over your workspace could be an empty box.

A special workspace holding several apps shows each app's icon in the sidebar, one under the other, instead of a generic grid. An open one leaves a small dot where it sits, and its card slides along when you switch workspaces instead of jumping.

Settings is rebuilt. It grows out of the sidebar on the screen you are using instead of opening as a separate window, and it stays open while you work in other windows. Its X or the settings corner closes it. Settings are sorted into ten categories, each opening on an overview, and the search box finds any setting by name.
Pointing at a setting shows what it does, the config.json key it writes if it has one, and a moving preview of that part of the shell. The last changes you made are listed with an undo button.

Changes to your screens' arrangement, resolution, scale and rotation wait until you press Apply. A new resolution, scale or rotation then asks to be kept, and goes back by itself after 15 seconds if you do not answer.
Some settings are marked new. You can set them and the panel remembers your choice, but nothing in the shell acts on them yet. They start working in later updates.

banditshell panel settings open takes a category, a page or any setting's config key, so banditshell panel settings open sidebar.update opens straight at that row. The old page names, like wifi or keybinds, still work.
The shell keeps the values of the new settings, and your recent changes, in ~/.local/state/banditshell/settings.json.

Updating installs exactly the version the update menu found. When it cannot, the menu says why in plain words instead of showing a line of git output: it names the files you edited that are in the way, or says that GitHub could not be reached or that this copy has changes of its own. A check that hangs now gives up after a few minutes.

The update icon above the clock now shows only when there is something to do: an update to get, a restart to finish one, or a problem. The rest of the time it is hidden, and What's new opens from the clock instead. To keep the icon all the time, or hide it even then, set Update button under Settings, Desktop, Sidebar. Settings, System, Updates has a button to check for updates.
config.json has a new key, sidebar.update. The default, new, shows the update icon only when there is something to do. always keeps it there, and never hides it even when an update is waiting.

Tab completion for banditshell now stays current in every terminal. Until now, after an update only the first terminal to press Tab learned the new commands, and terminals already open kept suggesting old ones, like banditshell try, until you restarted them. A terminal opened before this update needs exec zsh or exec bash once; after that it keeps up by itself.

The banditshell command is regrouped so it starts with the thing you want, then what to do with it: banditshell panel launcher toggle, banditshell screen border off, banditshell wallpaper next, banditshell clock timer start 10m. Plain banditshell lists 17 commands instead of 30, banditshell <command> help shows what one takes, and a command on its own, like banditshell screen, shows how that thing is right now. Your keybinds keep working as they are; the update menu offers to rewrite them to the new form, and banditshell doctor binds rewrite does the same.

Volume and locking are no longer banditshell commands, because wpctl and loginctl already do them: an old banditshell volume or lock command, typed or bound, now runs the matching wpctl or loginctl command. The sound menu, the media panel and the lock screen work as before.
The commands for working on the shell moved under banditshell dev: dev try, dev back, dev build, dev test, dev check, and the previews under dev preview.
banditshell screenshot full saves the whole desktop to your screenshots folder, next to the region screenshots from screenshot save and screenshot copy.

The wallpaper picker sits lower and smaller. The wallpaper you are on is in the middle, and the others are cropped strips beside it that never overlap and shrink away toward the ends, the whole row within 80% of the screen's width.

While the picker is open, the wallpaper you are looking at blooms in over your windows from the bottom edge, so you see it exactly as it will look. Everything behind the picker is dimmed, and the cards and controls cast shadows.
Colour swatches above the picker show only the wallpapers of that colour, and the search button (or /) filters them by name.
Below the picker: the wallpaper's name, resolution, kind and position, with shuffle, fits-this-screen, this-or-every-screen and Set buttons. Each has a tooltip.
The ring around the wallpaper you already have is gone. A ring now appears only while you move with the arrow keys.
Set, or Enter, always applies now, so choosing Every screen works without first moving to a different wallpaper.
The shell keeps each wallpaper's colour groups in a small cache file, ~/.cache/banditshell/wallpaper-colours.json.

banditshell try needs less typing. Bare, it takes the only worktree there is, or lists them numbered and asks which one. With a name, a number from that list or any unique part of a branch name works, so banditshell try 2 or banditshell try wall is enough, and Tab completes worktree names.

banditshell try runs a git worktree of the shell on your desktop in place of your installed copy, so you can try a branch before it is merged: banditshell try <branch>, or bare from inside the worktree. Bare anywhere else, it lists every worktree and marks the one running. banditshell back puts your installed copy back. While you are trying one, banditshell restart restarts it, and a worktree that fails to load puts you back on your installed copy by itself.

Leaving streamer mode now takes the band away and gives your other screens their frame back. The shell follows hypr-mode's streamer switch on every Hyprland reload, so Super+Ctrl+K turns it on and off without anything else to set up; banditshell set stream on without hypr-mode's streamer mode lasts only until the next reload.

Two config.json keys are gone: button.scale, because button labels now use the shell's three font sizes, and files.text, because Files text is the small size scaled by its zoom. The shell drops them from your config by itself; if you had changed either, that size no longer applies.
All text in the shell now comes in the same three sizes, so a few button labels change size slightly.
The dictation pill's language tag sits centred beside the bars again.

Starting the shell no longer writes your saved brightness to the monitors. On a Samsung Odyssey that write made the monitor reset, and the compositor crashed with it; the saved level now only shows on the slider, and the monitors get a new brightness only when you change it.

Six config.json keys are gone along with what used them: apps.claude (the app-icon asker), cheatsheet.symbols, and volume.grabFraction, volume.linger, volume.meterGlyphs and volume.railWidth (the old volume rail). The shell drops them from your config by itself. If you had changed volume.grabFraction or volume.linger, the value does not carry over: set screen.grabFraction or screen.linger instead.

Streamer mode for a portrait screen: banditshell set stream on DP-1 puts a band across the top of that screen with your OBS controls, each screen's workspaces and windows, network, sound and the clock, and its menus drop down under the item you click. banditshell set stream off ends it, and a restart keeps whichever you set.

The band's OBS deck: go live and end the stream (each takes a second click within three seconds), record, watch the bitrate and dropped frames while live, switch scenes, and show or hide the camera and the screen capture or mute the mic and desktop audio for viewers only. It talks to OBS's WebSocket server with the password OBS already has, and only while streamer mode is on.

While streaming, every other screen keeps its launcher, notch and pop-ups but reserves no space and draws no frame, so no window moves. Notifications and the keyring prompt go to the band's screen, where viewers cannot read them.

The dictation pill tucks out of the way when the pointer comes near and drops back when it leaves, costs far less to draw while you talk, and shows the language as a small tag beside the bars. While streaming it is a smaller, rounder capsule that floats below the edge.
Quick controls: a card on the right edge with sound, brightness and warmth, in place of the old volume rail.

Security fixes: the 802.1X Wi-Fi password reaches NetworkManager on stdin instead of a command line other programs can read, notification and other untrusted text renders as plain text (notification bodies keep bold, italic and underline), the keyring prompt names the program that asks, and the lock screen checks the account the shell runs as.
The lock screen locks before the machine sleeps, stays locked through a shell reload, and after three wrong passwords makes you wait 5 seconds, doubling up to a minute.
The shell does less while idle: Wi-Fi scans only while a network list is on screen, panels and Settings pages are built when first opened, and timers run only while something is moving.
Files and the built-in terminal: typed paths are quoted for the shell, names read as UTF-8, a paste can no longer break out of bracketed paste, and the terminal redraws only the rows that changed.
Log out ends this session instead of every session you have open.
banditshell completions install sets up zsh and bash completion generated from the CLI's own help, and banditshell check compiles every QML file and runs the tests.

New config.json keys arrive by themselves: stream (enabled, screen, height) for streamer mode, eight clock settings, cheatsheet.blocked and cheatsheet.keyboard, and screen settings for the quick controls' brightness and warmth. Nothing to do.

The source tree is reorganised around how you would look for things: the preview windows moved out of the repo root into previews/ behind a small router, and the jargon names became the words you would actually search for - Notifications, Calculator, SystemInfo, SummonZone, the alphabet launcher, SquircleRect. Nothing about how the shell looks or behaves moved with them.

The shell is now fully legible to the QML language server: every folder carries a qmldir and the LSP's import path is wired up, so code completion finds your own singletons and the editor's warning floor went from thousands to the few that can be kept honest. If you add a QML file, run scripts/qmldirs.sh once.
Internal: the source code shed its comment essays, cut to bare minimum, with no change to anything the shell does. Your config and setup are untouched; anyone reading the code can read it again.

Bare mode now squares the windows too (rounding and both gaps, outer and inner, go to zero), and the shell applies the compositor half itself: on the toggle, on every boot, and again after every compositor reload while bare, so the state comes back from a reboot whole instead of half-applied. Toggling back reloads the compositor, which returns your config's gaps and rounding to every open window at once.

Bare mode: the whole chrome can go off at once, every screen. Band, sidebar, reserved space and the invisible edge grabs all stand down, leaving the wallpaper and your windows; the shell still answers every keybind. Super+Shift+K toggles it, and runs the compositor's gap flip beside it so the windows sit flush.
One new config.json key, edge.bare, holds the switch. It is off by default and your config gains it by itself; nothing to do.

The sidebar can now be hidden on individual monitors. The Monitors page has a Sidebar switch for the selected one, and Super+K toggles the column on the monitor you are on; hidden means fully, with the windows taking the width back.

Two new config.json keys hold the same setting: sidebar.enabled, the default every screen follows, and sidebar.perScreen, which holds only the monitors that disagree. Your config gains them by itself; nothing to do.
